newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Experience vacuum threatens Singapore insurers.
newsitem.headline: Experience vacuum threatens Singapore insurers.

text.p: Singapore's booming insurance sector is facing the threat of an experience vacuum, according to the head of the Singapore College of Insurance (SCI).

SCI director Karine Kam says the industry has been hit by "musical chair syndrome" -- job and employer-hopping by ambitious junior and middle managers in search of executive titles and huge pay rises.
And this is coming at a critical time for Singapore's rapidly expanding insurance industry, Kam told Reuters in an interview on Friday.
"This could be a problem now that we are embarking on the next stage of our development," she said.
Her concerns reflect those of Singapore insurance chiefs who see ambitious young managers tempted by big-buck pay packets and the chance to move up the career ladder.

Already resigned to paying spiralling wages for promising, but inexperienced recruits, some senior managers now face the stark choice of promoting people faster than their experience would ordinarily dictate, or risk losing them altogether.
It is a choice that worries them.

"What happens when the market softens and claims come in while inexperienced underwriters are being promoted in heavy numbers?" asked one senior manager who declined to be identified. Plunging profits seems the inevitable answer.
But the thirst for promising people across all industry sectors in Singapore, from graduates to middle managers in their early 30s, seems unquenchable.

The problem is exacerbated by the fact that Singapore has virtually no unemployment. Changing career paths is not a problem, particularly in financial services where the country has built a thriving industry.
Kam said insurers find it tough to compete with the image of high-flying wheeler-dealing on the international stock market.

"In insurance you need to be slower in terms of career growth," she says and persuading ambitious youngsters they need years of field experience to respond successfully to the variety of claims and underwriting cases they will face is not easy.
But Kam said Singapore was already working to bridge the experience gap and raise the industry's professional profile by launching insurance-based degrees through its further education institutions.
"Insurance used to be a sub-discipline of a finance degree, but now it is held as an equivalent," she says.
In addition, she says the SCI is working on developing its own masters degree in conjunction with a U.S. university which could be unveiled in 1997.
But Kam said the industry must be more proactive about its human resource problems.

"The industry must be more forthcoming about suggesting the skills areas where it thinks there is a shortage. Insurers fund the expenditure of this college and the companies must make sure they are getting value from us," she says.
